# Dual-State Dependency Boundary Incident Postmortem

## Preserve the evidence first, rather than picking a state first

This postmortem documents an anomaly in cargo deny · Dependency Boundary Audit that could easily be obscured by "the page has already recovered." The dependency sources for the same object are established through lock and license, and continue to affect adoption scope and exit responsibilities. When the anomaly occurred, the current entry point reported different current revision values at two points in time; the old records and the recovered page were both still available. Readers who open only one of them could easily assume that the other is outdated noise, or conversely, that the recovered path had never had a problem.

The earliest draft did not attempt to provide a complete account of the cause. It recorded only one direct observation: the target filter differed from the old record; further retries were then stopped, and the entry-point version and original input were saved; after the release candidate, the original path could be restored; the change in the CI artifact remained unexplained. This sequence remains the starting point for this page. It shows that recovery had already occurred, and also that there was no evidence at the time tying that recovery to any particular cause.

The material added later did not change the anomaly itself, but only made its boundaries clearer. The page prompt for the exit action had lagged behind the actual state; after switching accounts or workspaces, the path would stop at the exit entry point; an adjacent current revision could serve as a comparison, but initially, only the first path difference should be examined. None of these can be taken to mean "the cause has been found."

## The shape of the anomaly

"Dual-state" here does not mean that the object itself simultaneously had two different dependency graphs, nor does it mean that either lock or license must have been rewritten. What is known is this: the current entry point led to different current revision values at two points in time, while the previously saved records were not overwritten by the entry-point update. As a result, from a reader's perspective, the same object presented two states that could be referenced.

This distinction matters. A dependency boundary audit does not merely display a list of names; it continues to assess adoption scope and exit responsibilities based on the dependency sources established through lock and license. If the current entry point leads readers to a different revision, they may adopt different sources on that basis, interpret the scope along different paths, or reach different stopping points when exiting. The anomaly therefore affects the chain of reasoning, not merely a page title.

On the other hand, the available material does not support a broader conclusion. There is no evidence that the entire `crate graph` was in an incorrect state. The observation at T+07 instead showed that `crate graph` was still normal at the time; this kept the investigation from lumping all dependency-graph phenomena together as one issue. Nor is there evidence that adjacent projects underwent the same change. This page does not extrapolate results from adjacent paths into project-level conclusions.

Still less can "the other entry point is normal" be taken to mean that the original anomaly did not exist. Both states had been observed, and the original record had also been valid evidence of the incident state. The recovered page fixed the path visible at the time, but did not automatically account for the intervening changes that led to the entry-point discrepancy.

## The sequence of records at the time

| Stage | Preserved information | What could be said at the time | What could not be said at the time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial discovery | The current entry point did not match the old record, and the target filter differed | The entry-point presentation and the original record were not directly interchangeable | The difference was caused by the target filter |
| Preserving the original state | The original input and entry-point version were not overwritten by later operations | The original reading location could still be revisited later | All conditions could already be reproduced |
| Initial comparison | `crate graph` did not show the same anomaly | The issue did not manifest as a failure of the entire dependency graph | All other paths were normal |
| Further narrowing | `policy edge` appeared at the comparison point | It could serve as a point for further comparison | It was the root cause |
| Path restoration | The original path was restored after the release candidate | The path was successfully followed again using Fang Ke | The changes to the CI artifact had been explained |

This table preserves the relative strength of the initial assessments. The statement in the draft that "the target filter differs from the old record" cannot be removed, because that was the starting point for recognizing the anomaly; however, it was no longer included as a cause in later conclusions. Similarly,`policy edge` once helped narrow the scope of comparison, but there was not enough supporting material for it to serve as the root cause.

To avoid mistaking relative times for a complete schedule, T+00, T+07, T+18, T+31 indicate only the sequence in the records captured at the time. The existing early drafts still lack specific timestamps, and no dates were fabricated to fill the blanks left there. The later card records include their respective operation times, but they are later additions and should not be retroactively treated as details already known at the draft stage.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> EntrySplit: Current entry point differs between the two points in time
    EntrySplit --> EvidenceSaved: Original record and entry-point version retained
    EvidenceSaved --> Narrowed: crate graph comparison did not show the same behavior
    Narrowed --> PathRestored: Path recovered after release candidate
    Narrowed --> CauseOpen: Source of the difference unconfirmed
    PathRestored --> CauseOpen: Recovery does not establish attribution
    CauseOpen --> Narrowed: Continue comparisons when a new case is available
```

The "CauseOpen" in the diagram is not an alias for a to-do state, but the actual stopping point for this incident: the available material is sufficient to explain what happened, when recovery had already occurred, and which conclusions do not hold; it is not sufficient to explain why a specific change caused the current entry point to point to a different revision.

## Why the initial attribution did not hold up

The initial draft recorded target filter as the earliest point of inconsistency. That step itself was not wrong: if the current entry point differs from the old record, it is natural to first look at the directly visible filtering differences. The problem is that direct visibility does not imply causality. What could later be confirmed was only that the original path had recovered, not whether the change to target filter had caused the entry point to differ, nor whether there was a direct connection between it and the change to the CI artifact.

Another shortcut that did not hold up was treating screenshots as sufficient incident evidence. The earlier secondhand reports contained only screenshots, lacked account- or workspace-level context, and did not record which entry point they had stopped at. They therefore could not explain why another path worked, much less compare whether different people and different workspaces had reached the same exit entry point. Screenshots can still serve as corroborating evidence that "an anomaly was observed", but cannot by themselves support conclusions about the scope of impact or the cause.

The third common misjudgment is treating recovery as an explanation of the fix. The release candidate restored the original path, which is the most direct outcome for users; but that recovery was not accompanied by material that could explain the change to the CI artifact. Adding a particular implementation, command, or version as the root cause here would only turn later hopes into a conclusion about the incident.

Therefore, this postmortem retains three levels:

- **Observed behavior**: The current entry point shows different current revisions at two points in time, and both the original record and the recovery page exist.
- **Recovery result**: After the release candidate, the previously affected paths can be restored.
- **Unconfirmed causes**: Where the entry-point differences begin, why the CI artifact changed, and whether there is a causal relationship between the target filter and the differences.

These three layers cannot be collapsed into a single statement that "the issue is resolved". The first two address the observed state and the usage outcome, respectively, while the third remains open.

## Boundaries Exposed by Exit Actions

The subsequent CDPA-010 does not invent a new cause for the incident after the fact, but fills in how the exit side should preserve a record of the observed state. This card requires a walkthrough from the exit-action entry point using an ordinary account, recording the point of rejection and the fallback action. This requirement addresses a shortcoming in the earlier screenshot evidence: simply saying "cannot proceed" is of no value; at a minimum, we need to know which entry point stopped the process and what fallback was actually used afterward.

One sequence of changes in the record is worth retaining separately. When the expiration action had already become invalid, the entry-point prompt on the page had not yet been updated to match; the prompt was later changed back to pending update, and the invalid expiration action was no longer presented to newcomers to click. There are two distinct questions here: whether the action can still be executed, and whether the page still treats it as an executable entry point. The former is the operational state, and the latter is the navigation state. When they are out of sync, readers may mistakenly believe they are entering the current path, when in fact they may stop at an action that is already invalid.

This also explains why this page does not describe "cleaning up old navigation" as the entire set of measures for resolving the dual-state issue. Expired current entry points should be cleaned up, but the original incident record and dates must remain available for lookup. Removing entry-point prompts can reduce wrong turns; deleting old records would deprive later readers of a reference for comparison. The scope of CDPA-023 is precisely the former: cleaning up expired navigation while keeping the original "cargo deny · Dependency Boundary Audit the same object appears in two states" record available for lookup.

The walkthrough using an ordinary account is the only path in these materials for which recording the point of rejection and the fallback action is explicitly required. It cannot be replaced by a path using higher privileges. A successful walkthrough by an administrator or in another workspace only shows that the process did not stop at the same point in that context; it does not erase the behavior seen by an ordinary account at the exit entry point.

## Source Tracing and Adjacent Comparisons

CDPA-011 requires tracing back along the revision of `cargo-deny-supply-boundary` to the earliest source that can be reconstructed, rather than guessing from the displayed text. This action fills a gap in the source-tracing method, rather than treating page text as a fact about the version. When the revision shown at the current entry point does not match the saved record, the displayed text is likely only the starting point for the investigation; determining whether the two are actually related still requires tracing back along the revision.

In this work item, after switching to a different account or workspace, the path stopped at the exit entry point. The difference was later recorded in the card, and the stopping point was still the exit entry point. This record supports only a limited conclusion: the account or workspace was context that needed to be retained at the time and could not be omitted from screenshots. It does not support "the account or workspace is the source of the dual states," because no material shows that the different revisions of the current entry point after the switch resulted from this.

The scope of the comparison between CDPA-024 was also deliberately narrow: select an adjacent current revision whose path can be completed, and compare only the first path difference. This was not intended to make the adjacent path the baseline ground truth, but to avoid introducing multiple differences in a single comparison. If the first difference already explains the stopping point, preserve it first; if it does not, wait for new evidence from the environment rather than guessing the subsequent path during a single review.

The working sequence derived from these two cards is: first confirm which source the revision you are looking at can be traced back to; then take only the first path difference from adjacent revisions whose paths can be completed; finally, retain the account or workspace, the stopping position at the exit entry point, and the actual fallback together. This sequence is intended to keep the subject of the investigation stable and does not mean that the root cause of this incident has already been found.

## How Recovery Was Determined

Early records explicitly stated that recovery was possible with the release candidate. Later versions did not change this, but added a limitation: the recovery assessment covered only the originally affected paths. It did not cover all sources or all adoption scopes, nor did it guarantee that every exit entry point had been updated.

Recovery was determined by whether the path could be completed again, not by the last line of green output. Earlier material had already shown that retaining only the cleaned-up green results would lose the entry point, account or workspace, and stopping position at the time of the anomaly. For this incident, a green result can prove that a particular attempt did not fail at the original position; it cannot retroactively prove that the two different current revisions never appeared, or that the old records were already meaningless at the time.

The material that still needs to be retained after recovery can be listed as a set of copies captured from the environment:

1. The current entry point when the difference appeared, and the current revision visible at the time;
2. The original record that was not overwritten;
3. The page after the path was restored;
4. The point of denial and the actual fallback action during a test run with a regular account;
5. If adjacent revisions are compared, record only the first path difference.

This is not intended to create an abstract process, but is necessary because this postmortem has already shown that omitting any one of these items changes which questions can be answered later. Without the original record, the two states cannot be compared; without the recovery page, the earlier incident state cannot be distinguished from an ongoing problem; without the account or workspace, the stopping behavior at the exit entry point cannot be explained; introducing multiple path differences at once reintroduces variables that cannot be distinguished from one another.

CI artifact remains an unconfirmed item. It appears in the early records because the materials from before and after recovery show it changing; however, there is no complete chain connecting this change to the current entry point, lock, license, or target filter. It is retained here to prevent it from later being mistaken for a factor that has already been ruled out or confirmed when related materials are reviewed.

## Actual Scope of Impact

This incident provides no evidence that dependency sources were uniformly replaced, nor any evidence that the license determination itself became invalid. What is known is that the source information formed around lock and license is used to determine the scope of adoption and exit responsibility, while the dual state of the current entry point interferes with this determination.

The scope of adoption was affected because the reading order diverged: some people started from the saved old record, while others started from the updated current entry point. If they correspond to different current revision values, they may produce different interpretations of the source from the same object. Exit responsibility was affected similarly: when the page prompt still pointed to an expiration action, readers might try to complete the exit through an invalidated entry point; the evidence from a regular account shows that at least one attempt stopped at the exit entry point.

But this does not mean that all adoption and exit actions failed. Existing records do not quantify the scope, nor do they confirm the behavior of all accounts, workspaces, or adjacent revisions. Treating the unknown scope as affecting everything would make this page more certain than the observed situation; describing the single path after recovery as full recovery would likewise go beyond the materials.

`crate graph` remained normal in an early comparison and is a useful counterexample. It reminds investigators not to automatically interpret differences between object entry points as an anomaly in the dependency graph as a whole. A counterexample is not evidence of root cause, but it keeps the impact scope at a supportable level.

## Retained Earlier Judgments

The following two passages are retained in their historical context and must not be used as current conclusions.

> **Early assessment, later unconfirmed:** The target filter differs from the old record and may be the explanation for the dual state.
>
> This sentence records the most direct difference at the time of the initial discovery. Subsequent materials did not establish the causal relationship implied by "may," so it cannot be used to close the investigation into the CI artifact, the entry prompt, or the revision source.

> **Simplified statement during recovery, too narrow in scope:** The release candidate has been restored, so the incident is over.
>
> This was later revised to: the original path was restored, but why the current entry point once pointed to a different revision remains unconfirmed; the page prompt for the exit action also lagged behind the actual state. Recovery can end the urgent blockage affecting the user path, but it cannot erase the original observed state.

Retaining the earlier judgments is not intended to let them continue to be cited, but to explain why later versions separate "phenomenon," "recovery," and "cause." This separation comes from the materials of this incident, not from an abstract document-formatting requirement.

## Relationship to Related Cards

CDPA-010 records a regular account's walkthrough of the exit action, along with the saved rejection point and fallback action. It supplements the observed situation at the exit entry point.

CDPA-011 documents provenance tracing for revision `cargo-deny-supply-boundary`, as well as the case where account or workspace differences stop at the exit entry point. It fills in provenance lookup and context.

CDPA-023 handles navigation for expired current entry points, while requiring the original record and date to remain searchable. It fills in historical retention after navigation cleanup.

CDPA-024 constrains comparisons of adjacent current revisions to look only at the first path difference. It fills in the comparison scope.

These cards can all help with their respective issues, but none replaces this page's confirmation of the root cause. Their relationship to the incident record should remain limited to navigation and local actions, and card status changes must not be rewritten as incident causality.

DOC-32 handles the exit-window checklist for cargo-deny-supply-boundary. The two pages will be adjacent in terms of exit responsibility, but should not copy one another: DOC-32 provides executable checks and stop points; this page retains why a single entry-state divergence makes exit decisions unreliable, and what should still remain after recovery.

## Still unconfirmed items

- The direct trigger causing the current entry point to produce different current revisions at two points in time has not been confirmed.
- There is only an observed temporal ordering between the target filter and this difference, with no confirmed causal relationship.
- Why the CI artifact changed has not been confirmed.
- Why differences in account or workspace caused the attempt to stop at the exit entry point has not been confirmed; what is known is that this stop point was recorded.
- The first path difference between adjacent current revisions can continue to provide a comparison, but no evidence shows that it explains this dual state.

These items should not be backfilled as conclusions about a lock, license, or page change. If new on-site evidence becomes available later, it should still first be compared against the saved original record, recovery page, and entry version; without all three, it is difficult to determine whether the new result is reproducing the old anomaly, showing navigation lag, or observing another independent path.

## Archive location

The incident's long-term entry point is `docs/adj-cargo-deny/incidents/cargo-deny-dependency-boundary-audit-two-states-for-one-object.md`. That location preserves the original record, recovery page, and the state in which the cause remains unconfirmed alongside them. When cleaning up expired navigation, this entry must not be allowed to disappear with it; it is the only reference point for later distinguishing between "the old page is still searchable" and "the old entry is still recommended for use".

This review ends here. What can currently be confirmed is that the path has been restored, the previous state can still be viewed, and the exit entry point was previously affected by account or workspace context; what cannot currently be confirmed is how the two current revision variants were produced and why the changes to the CI artifact occurred.

The row for the old entry point comes from a canceled investigation: at the time, the issue was observed only at the entry point that was no longer supported. This does not establish that the present entry point has the same problem, and the row should not be removed from the table. When someone comes in through an old link, first confirm which entry point they are looking at; if it is still the old entry point, just record the behavior as observed without repackaging it as a new release incident.

The second result for the current revision was once missing; the handoff was later confirmed to have taken place. Handling was reassigned to that cycle's on-call contact because the previous owner was not covering that cycle. This records the on-call handoff arrangement, not long-term individual ownership. That review had little effect on the table: another person could reach the exit entry point again, but the review did not designate a new owner for explaining the behavior. flowchart TD
    A[Issue received] --> B{Exit action expired?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Interim maintainer handles expiry action]
    B -- No --> D{Involves explaining behavior?}
    D -- Yes --> E[Route to original owner]

That assumption explains why the split was proposed; it does not prove that the split route was better.

Those in favor of keeping `evidence ledger` also had specific concerns. A continuous record at least kept the input, observations, and explanations added later together; splitting it into an entry point and a graph could leave maintainers tracking two places at once and end up breaking a single failure sample into disconnected fragments. Different failure exits for the two sections did not automatically mean that two entry points should become the default. The old draft did not resolve this objection, so `crate graph` remained only a candidate name.

A two-week trial was proposed at one point. The first group would still enter through the record `not-adopted-LICENSE-MIT-quality-signal-dashboard-route`, while the other group would use the candidate `crate graph`. The comparison would use the same input and observation window, changing only the recording entry point. The plan was to record the raw input, version, and first visible result first each time, then check whether failure samples, regression layers, and the attribution of unstable signals were easier to identify than with the original route.

Here, "the same input" did not mean the two sides had to reach the same conclusion. It was only meant to avoid a situation where one side received material earlier and the other later, and the difference in observation times was ultimately misreported as a difference between entry points. The first visible result was to be recorded separately because explanations added later could make a record that had initially looked complete read coherently; the trial was still meant to test whether the material could be found at the outset, not whether it could be explained coherently after being organized.

The review called for an input pointing the other way precisely to avoid comparing only material consistent with the original assessment; that field is still blank here. Without that opposing input, even if the split route appeared to make things easier to locate, it might merely have placed familiar failure samples where they were easier to read. The old draft did not treat this gap as something display labels could fill.

The plan had no start date either. A long-term maintainer had not been chosen, so it did not take it as given that someone would keep organizing the results from both sides. The two weeks mentioned in the old draft were a proposed observation period, not a release cadence; the candidate entry point could not be called the new default before that period ended. Anyone maintaining this record later should still treat it as a record of the proposal at the time, not as documentation of a completed migration.

When judging whether the trial was valid, it was not enough to look only at whether the last run was green. A single green result might not have reached the original failure exit; changing only display labels would not change where the material was placed. If the original `policy edge` could not be restored after backing out, even the return point for the comparison would be unclear. If locating material was no faster and incorrect assessments had not decreased, that too would be insufficient grounds for retaining the candidate route.

At the time, restoring the old entry point was tentatively set as the minimum action for backing out. Here, "restoring" only meant starting from the original record again; it did not mean that a decision had already been made on how to handle derived records produced during the trial. Whether those records should be retained, whether the results of `crate graph` should be saved separately, and which layer the failure samples should ultimately be assigned to were questions the old draft did not answer. Filling these gaps with a fixed procedure would change this page's original status as a proposal.

Two other boundaries remained unresolved. The callers using `license expression` at the time had not been verified, so this could not be used to infer which locations the split would affect; if the entry point changed during the trial, numbers from before and after the change could not simply be combined to establish a trend. Supporters of the split saw this as a reason to also flag entry-point changes, while opponents thought it increased the chance of both sets of records drifting at the same time.

At the time, then, this route remained at "can be tried, but not finalized on this basis." Keeping the original record as the entry point had the advantage of keeping input, observations, and explanations in one place; a separate entry point had the advantage that where failure samples ended up would not have to depend on explanations added later. Neither side made a decisive case with the material available at the time. Not adopting the route did not mean the split hypothesis had been disproven; it meant only that it had not yielded comparison results sufficient to replace the original entry point.

If this is discussed again, the comparison should be rebuilt from the original entry point, raw input, and first visible result, before deciding whether the opposing input is sufficient to start the trial. At handoff, have the person handing over and the person taking over each state the entry point and result they saw; if their accounts differ, write that in a new addendum rather than rewriting the old assessment in this working-draft. This page remains background on a route that was not adopted; it does not present the candidate entry point as a released capability.

# Policy Graph Window Decision Record

This record captures a limited trade-off Northstar Forge made for the Policy Graph release window. People have continued to refer back to it, usually to check why the window adjustment under discussion was not included directly in the approved scope at the time. The wording and reservations from that review are retained here; they describe the objects that review could account for, not a broad judgment about every later release.

The conclusion in the first draft did not change: retain the current bans entry point, with approval limited to the parts already covered by the available material. The follow-up review did not change the window adjustment from "not yet supported" to "supported," either. This choice was not made because the entry point's name was inherently safer, but because the available material still lined up: the repository object the entry point referred to, the repository path, and the Cargo graph and diagnostics tied to that scope.

## The Two Options Compared at the Time

Keeping the current bans entry point meant not moving the boundary of the objects under discussion in this round. It allowed the already-linked repository path to remain the starting point for discussion, and kept the graph and diagnostics describing the same scope. The other option was to adjust the release window, changing the boundary of coverage for this round. That option had its uses, but once the boundary moved, opinions favoring it in the discussion were not enough to establish that the old material still referred to the same object.

The review material specified this order:

> link the repository path before the discussion thread

This was not a post-meeting formatting requirement. Finding the repository path first establishes which repository object the opinions in the discussion thread refer to; looking at the Cargo graph and diagnostics next establishes whether they still connect to the discussion at hand. If the window were expanded first and the path supplied afterward, the same bans entry point could be read as referring to different objects in different contexts.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B[Current bans entry point] --> P[repository path]
  P --> T[discussion thread]
  P --> G[Cargo graph]
  G --> D[diagnostics]
  D --> A[Approved scope]
  W[Adjust release window] --> U[Not yet covered]
```

"Not yet covered" in the diagram was the reason for that choice, not a permanent rejection of window adjustments. The material also required:

> Treat the Cargo graph and its diagnostics as evidence that must survive a context change.

This did not require the graph or diagnostics to remain unchanged forever. It required that, when the discussion moved into a new context, the object and scope they originally described could still be identified. That review did not have material establishing this continuity, so the adjusted window was not included in the approved scope.

## Decision and Reservations

The decision was to continue using the current bans entry point. The parts that could be matched across the repository path, Cargo graph, and diagnostics would be handled within the original scope. A window adjustment could not automatically receive the same conclusion just because someone in the discussion supported it; it needed material that would allow the object to remain identifiable within the new boundary.

The objections were not removed. They remind readers that alternatives were compared at the time, rather than proving that the current entry point is better in every situation. Reading "do not adjust yet" as "must not adjust" would miss the decision's most important premise: the approved scope follows objects that can be cross-checked, not the term release window.

## Follow-up Review Note

For this note, the review traced back through `src/lib.rs` and the invocation names used at the time. The file location helped anchor the topic back to the repository path, but did not resolve all the questions. Still unconfirmed: which paths had already been explicitly linked before the discussion began; whether the available Cargo graph and diagnostics could carry through the proposed context change; and whether the same bans entry point could lead back to the same object after the adjustment.

These questions received no new affirmative answers, so the original decision was retained. For the dependency audit rotation handoff, see DOC-44; that material covers the handoff process. This page records only the release window trade-off and the reasons the alternative was not adopted at the time.

bans public entry

hit src/licenses.rs

one direct caller

first real consumer of documentation cleanup
```

## What to Look At First

`src/licenses.rs` is the actual landing point for this review. When entering files from hits on `licenses` and related notes, first confirm two things: whether what you are looking at is a call relationship or just text about a similar topic; and whether you can identify a direct caller from this position. Only put it in the path if you can identify the caller. Files with only the same name, similar comments, or an adjacent directory are not the next hop.

This distinction was not stated clearly enough in the first pass. The initial view was that files near a hit on `bans` could be used to continue toward documentation cleanup. The narrower judgment retained after review is this: same-named files can help with locating things, but without a call edge they are only signposts. Otherwise, readers will mistake "adjacent in search results" for "connected at runtime."

The release freeze note serves only as a locator. It can help place a passage back in the release freeze context of the time and assess why this path was retained; it does not prove that new calls exist between files, nor does it turn the note's wording into code behavior. If the note's wording differs from `src/licenses.rs`, prioritize tracing back along the actual entry and direct caller. Leave anything that cannot be tied to a call edge where it is.

## How Far Is Enough

The "actual entry" here is not every related documentation cleanup page. It is the first real consumer that can be confirmed starting from `bans`. Once you reach it, you can at least answer: where the entry starts, which direct caller picks up the path, and where the cleanup action is first consumed. Pages farther downstream may reference the same topic, but this page has no material that establishes them as a continuous relationship.

So do not mix together the following:

- `bans` itself, the public entry;
- the file location in `src/licenses.rs` used for tracing back;
- files with only similar names or wording and no call edge;
- the collaboration scope after the first real consumer of documentation cleanup.

The first two form a short, verifiable chain. The third is a search signpost, and the fourth has already crossed this page's local boundary. This distinction is more useful than adding more filenames, because another name does not make the call relationship any more certain.

The earlier record phrased "hit" almost as though it meant "enter." # CI runner maintenance window deviation retrospective

During the maintenance window, the visible result did not appear as originally planned. What we initially received was not a clear error, but a result that did not match the pre-window expectation; it was therefore recorded at the time as a runner maintenance deviation rather than a change to the license rules. The confirmation action stopped first when the result could not be compared; during the window, we did not continue interpreting the deviation as evidence that the rules had already changed.

## What happened at the time

- After the window began, the result seen during release confirmation did not match the original plan. When it was first discovered, no complete result snapshot was retained—only the assessment that the "results were inconsistent."
- The investigation first landed near the review diff hunk retained around `src/licenses.rs`. This was the viewing point found by following the call name at the time, not a conclusion about ownership of the problem; the file location alone cannot show whether the deviation occurred in the runner, the confirmation action, or the change being reviewed.
- After the temporary recovery, the visible result could again be compared with the original plan. The recovery only shows that the immediate blockage disappeared; it does not explain why the result initially diverged, and no complete record was left of "what the recovery action changed."

A control point was added during review: `link the repository path before the discussion thread`. Link the repository path to the discussion first so that later readers can identify exactly which part of the diff was being reviewed; if the search continues from only a call name, it is easy to mistake the review diff hunk in the file for the ownership of the problem. This addition addresses confusion at the investigation entry point, not the root cause, and does not rule out the maintenance window itself as a possible cause.

## Impact assessment at the time

Confirmation during the window was delayed; beyond that, this page does not extend the impact to other runners or other release candidates. The result after the temporary recovery was used to continue the plan within the window, but that was not used to declare the maintenance action entirely unrelated. Here, "recovery" only means that the visible result became comparable again; it does not mean that all relevant checks had been completed.

The old record tended to attribute the deviation to the maintenance window itself. That assessment is retained here because it explains why runner status was checked first at the time; it has not been confirmed by this retrospective. Whether the review diff hunk had a direct relationship to the deviation also remains unconfirmed. The path control point added later changed the search order but provided no new root-cause evidence.

Two items are still missing: the complete result snapshot from the initial discovery and what the temporary recovery actually changed. This page also does not record whether other runners experienced the same deviation.
